items.prompt: What is an AI language model built to produce?
choices: The most plausible-sounding next words
A fact confirmed against a database
The answer a human expert would give
A list of sources it has looked up
items.explanation: It predicts plausible continuations of text; it does not look a claim up before answering.

items.prompt: In the calculator story, what did the screen show for Tom's slipped keystroke?
choices: A red warning about his input
A blank screen until he rechecked
A blinking cursor beside the digits
A clean, confident 210
items.explanation: The display looked just as calm for the wrong number as for Priya's right one.

items.prompt: Which of these shows that an AI answer is true?
choices: Being worded in a confident, assured tone
Including precise and very specific details
Being checked against an independent source
Being grammatically perfect all the way through
items.explanation: Only a check says anything about truth; tone, detail and grammar describe the writing.

items.prompt: How does a wrong AI answer differ from a sloppy blog post?
choices: It always cites a fake source
It lacks the usual tells of shakiness
It is always shorter than the post
It is always flagged by the tool
items.explanation: A sloppy post shows its flaws; a wrong AI answer reads smooth and authoritative.

items.prompt: What numbers did Priya use for her rough check on the bill?
choices: About 80 divided by 4, so about 20
840 divided by 4, so about 210
84 divided by 40, so about 2
About 100 divided by 4, so about 25
items.explanation: Rounding 84 to 80 gives a quick estimate near 20, which exposes 210 as off by a factor of ten.

items.prompt: Who made the mistake in Tom's calculator story?
choices: The calculator, in its division
Priya, in her rough estimate
The restaurant, in the bill total
Tom, through a slipped keystroke
items.explanation: The calculator divided correctly; the wrong input was the problem, and nothing on screen showed it.

items.prompt: "Sounds sure of itself" is a property of what?
choices: Whether the claim was verified
The accuracy of its source
How the text reads
The age of the information
items.explanation: Confidence is a feature of the wording, not of any check behind it.

items.prompt: Does a named source in an AI answer make the claim true?
choices: Yes, any named source is proof
No, not until you open it and compare
Yes, if the source sounds official
Yes, if the name is a real organization
items.explanation: A citation is more generated text; the check is opening the source and confirming it says that.

items.prompt: Two assistants state the same claim, one in a hedged tone and one in a polished, confident tone. What does the tone difference tell you?
choices: The confident one is likelier true, since it was trained on facts
Nothing reliable, since tone is style and not verification
The hedged one is likelier true, since hedging signals care taken
Both are true only if each of them also names a source
items.explanation: Tone is a property of the wording. Neither tone is evidence that either claim was checked against anything.
items.reference:
Looks right vs. is checked
🗣️ Fluent, specific, confident: how the text reads
🔍 Compared with an independent source: whether it is true
🧮 Priya's rough check: 80 / 4 is about 20, so 210 is off
Why: fluency, detail and confidence describe the writing, so only an independent check says anything about the claim.
items.learnMore:
Fluency is not evidence

An AI model produces plausible-sounding text, and plausible text reads the same whether it is right or wrong. A wrong answer carries none of the tells a sloppy article does.

Common mistake

Reading a confident, detailed answer as if confidence were a measure of accuracy.
items.reflection: Think of a time a confident, well-delivered answer from any source turned out to be wrong. What would have made you check it before acting?

items.prompt: An AI answer has a precise number, a named guideline and a calm tone. Which one would actually move you toward trusting it?
choices: You opening the guideline and finding the number there
The number being stated precisely to two decimal places
The guideline being given an official-sounding long title
The tone staying calm and even throughout the whole answer
items.explanation: Precision, titles and calm are all text properties. Opening the guideline and confirming the number is the only action that touches truth.

Treat 210 as a draft and run a rough check before acting

The answer's quality did not decide the outcome; the check did

items.prompt: What is a load-bearing claim?
choices: One a real decision or later reasoning rests on
One that appears in the first sentence or two
One that the AI sounds most certain about here
One that comes with the longest explanation given
items.explanation: It is defined by what depends on it, not by its position, tone or length.

items.prompt: Which AI claim most deserves a check?
choices: A film's release year, asked out of curiosity
A fun fact to mention at a party
A synonym for a word in an email
A dose a parent is about to give
items.explanation: Safety is at stake there; the others change nothing important if they are off.

items.prompt: Which claim usually needs no check?
choices: A figure about to go into a budget
A legal deadline you plan around
Idle trivia nothing rides on
A safety instruction for a child
items.explanation: No decision depends on it, so a check would cost more than a mistake would.

items.prompt: What does a surprising claim earn?
choices: Immediate acceptance as new knowledge
Extra scrutiny, since errors hide there
No check, because surprise is a good sign
A re-ask to the same assistant
items.explanation: A claim you would have bet against is exactly where an error is most likely.

items.prompt: What should scale with the stakes?
choices: How much checking you do
How long the AI's answer is
How many AI tools you open
How polite your question sounds
items.explanation: More at stake means a more careful check before acting.

items.prompt: For a decision that is hard to undo, what does the table suggest?
choices: One quick glance at the answer, then acting on it
No check at all, if the AI sounds quite sure of it
A single rewording of the same question once again
More than one independent source, and slowing down
items.explanation: The harder a mistake is to reverse, the more checking it earns.

items.prompt: Why was it fine for Ines to skip checking "honey is a natural sweetener"?
choices: Natural sweeteners are always safe to give
The AI had cited a source for that line
Nothing she did that night depended on it
She already trusted the assistant a lot
items.explanation: Only the safety threshold was load-bearing, so only that claim earned a check.

items.prompt: Why is maximum suspicion of every sentence a problem?
choices: It makes true claims turn false
It is too slow to keep doing
It makes AI answers longer
It is only needed for trivia
items.explanation: A habit that is too costly gets dropped, which protects nobody.

items.prompt: An AI answer about planning a trip includes both a passport rule and a remark that the city is famous for its bridges. Which pairing is right?
choices: Load-bearing: the bridges remark; not load-bearing: the passport rule
Load-bearing: the passport rule; not load-bearing: the bridges remark
Both are load-bearing, because they came from the same answer
Neither is load-bearing, because both came from an assistant
items.explanation: The passport rule decides whether you can travel; the bridges remark changes nothing you do.
items.reference:
Scale the check to the stakes
🎲 Idle trivia: usually no check
💰 Money, a grade, safety: one independent source
🚫 Hard to undo: more than one source, and slow down
Why: you cannot check every sentence, so spend checks on the claims something real rests on.
items.learnMore:
Load-bearing claims

A load-bearing claim is one a decision or later reasoning will rest on. Surprising claims also earn extra scrutiny because errors tend to hide there.

Common mistake

Either checking nothing or trying to check every sentence with equal intensity.

The same, since all claims are equally uncertain
More, since agreement with you may be bias
None ever, since agreement with you proves it
items.explanation: Stakes and surprise both set the level. Here both are low, so a light touch fits.

They should have used fewer sources for each claim
Scrutiny was uniform instead of scaled to what mattered
They skipped asking the AI to cite its sources
items.explanation: The habit is picking the load-bearing claims; checking everything equally is not sustainable.

items.prompt: Where do the outsourcing trap and the accelerant loop split?
choices: At whether an independent check happens
At whether the AI answers quickly
At whether the question was well written
At whether the answer is long
items.explanation: Both start by asking; one adds the check, the other skips it.

items.prompt: Does the accelerant loop give up the AI's speed?
choices: Yes, it replaces the AI with manual research
Yes, it doubles the time of every question
Only when the answer turns out to be wrong
No, it keeps the speed and adds one step
items.explanation: The AI still supplies the fast first draft; the loop adds a small check.

items.prompt: In the outsourcing trap, an unverified claim ends up as what?
choices: A note flagged as uncertain
A claim awaiting an independent check
Part of what you believe
A claim discarded after a day
items.explanation: Without a check, an accepted answer simply becomes belief.

items.prompt: In the active column, how is an answer treated right after it arrives?
choices: As settled because it sounds informed
As a draft claim, not yet a fact
As wrong until proven right three times
As a source for other answers
items.explanation: Holding it as a draft is what leaves room for a check.

items.prompt: In the accelerant loop, what becomes belief?
choices: Only the checked version of the claim
Everything the AI said in the first answer
Everything except the numbers
Whatever matches your previous opinion
items.explanation: Confirmed, corrected or flagged-uncertain claims become belief; the rest stays tentative.

items.prompt: Ravi and Ines read the same answer. What separated their evenings?
choices: How much each knew about nutrition
Which assistant each one asked
How fluent the answer sounded to each
Accepted as fact versus held as a draft
items.explanation: Identical answer, identical question; one thirty-second check was the only difference.

items.prompt: What does the loop add back that the trap skips?
choices: A longer and more detailed first question
A second AI tool to ask the same thing
A specific check on the claims that matter
A rule against ever using AI tools at all
items.explanation: It is one step, not a ban or a bigger toolkit.

items.prompt: A month later, what has an unchecked claim in the passive column become?
choices: A flagged guess, kept clearly apart
Something you quietly "know"
A discarded draft, kept well out
A claim on a to-check list
items.explanation: Unverified claims drift into knowledge when nothing marks them as unchecked.

items.prompt: Student A uses an AI for a first overview, then checks the two claims her essay depends on. Student B copies the same overview in. What is the difference?
choices: A was slower overall, and B ended up learning more of the topic
A kept her judgment in use, and B outsourced her understanding
A used more AI tools than B did, and B used fewer of them overall
B kept her judgment in use, and A did not keep hers in use at all
items.explanation: Both gained speed; only A added the check that keeps understanding her own.
items.reference:
Same start, different loop
⚡ Accelerant: ask, check the claim that matters, believe the checked version
🕳️ Trap: ask, accept, believe the unchecked version
Why: the only difference between the two loops is whether an independent check happens before the claim becomes belief.
items.learnMore:
Accelerant vs. outsourcing

Both loops use the AI for speed. The accelerant loop adds one independent check on the load-bearing claim before it becomes belief, so your judgment keeps working.

Common mistake

Thinking the choice is between using AI and not using it.
items.reflection: Where in your own learning routine could a single check sit between "the answer arrived" and "I now believe it"?

No, since AI drafts can never be used at work at all
items.explanation: The loop needs a check on the claims decisions rest on; a tone read does not provide that.

items.prompt: What counts as an independent check?
choices: A source that shares none of the original's weakness
Any source that happens to agree with the AI answer
The same assistant asked the same thing a second time
A source the AI named but that you never actually opened
items.explanation: Independence means the check can fail in a different way.

items.prompt: Does asking the same assistant again count as an independent check?
choices: Yes, if you reword the question
Yes, if you ask it three times
Yes, if the new answer is longer
No, it can repeat the same mistake
items.explanation: The same tool tends to be wrong for the same reason.

items.prompt: An AI names a source. What is the check?
choices: Notice that a source was named in it
Ask the AI whether that source exists
Open the source and compare the claim
Copy the source name into your notes
items.explanation: A name is a pointer; the check is confirming the source says it.

items.prompt: Assume one independent check catches a wrong claim 65% of the time. What is the chance one check catches it?
items.explanation: That is the assumption itself, an illustrative teaching number.

items.prompt: Under that assumption, about what chance do two independent checks catch it?
Which independent check adds the most?
choices: The second
The fourth
The fifth
The first
items.explanation: It takes the chance from 0% to 65%; each later one adds less.

items.prompt: What kind of number is the 65% figure in this unit?
choices: A measured rate from real studies of AI
A guarantee that holds for any claim
An assumed teaching number, not measured
The rate at which AI answers are wrong
items.explanation: It is labeled as an assumption to show the shape of the returns.

items.prompt: What makes a pediatrician's own page a good check on a baby-feeding claim?
choices: It agrees with the AI answer given
It is authoritative for that very claim
It is just a webpage like any other
It is weaker than a second AI answer
items.explanation: A good check is independent and has a real reason to be right about this.

items.prompt: Under the 65% assumption with independent checks, what does a third check bring the total to, and what does it add over two?
choices: 95.7%, an added gain of about 22.8 points
95.7%, an added gain of about 7.9 points
98.5%, an added gain of about 2.8 points
87.8%, an added gain of about 7.9 points
items.explanation: Three checks give 1 - 0.35^3 = 0.957. Over two checks (87.8%) that adds about 7.9 points.
items.reference:
What counts as a check
❌ Ask the same assistant again
❌ Notice that a source was named
✅ Open the source and compare
✅ Read the owner's own page or docs
📉 Assumed 65% per check: 65, 87.8, 95.7, 98.5, 99.5
Why: a check helps only if it can fail differently from the original, and each extra independent check adds less than the one before.
items.learnMore:
Independent, authoritative, opened

An independent source does not share the original's weakness. The 65% catch rate and the 1 - 0.35^n curve are assumed teaching numbers, and they only hold if checks fail independently.

Common mistake

Counting rewordings of the same question as several checks.
items.reflection: Next time an AI names a source, what would opening it and comparing look like for the claim you care about?

It assumes any named source is always a real one
items.explanation: The multiplication only works if each check can fail separately; rewordings of the same question mostly fail together.

items.prompt: What is the average time complexity of Python's built-in sort?
choices: O(n log n)
O(n log log n)
O(n^2 log n)
items.explanation: Timsort is O(n log n) on average and in the worst case, so a fluent "linear" is wrong.

items.prompt: Name two reasonable checks for the sort-complexity claim.
choices: Asking the same assistant a second time or more
Counting the words in its long and detailed answer
Judging how confident its answer sounded to you
Official documentation, or a small timing test
items.explanation: Documentation or a timing experiment can fail differently from the assistant.

items.prompt: If a hard claim truly cannot be checked, what should you do?
choices: Treat it as true because it sounds right enough
Delete it and never use it again in any way
Label it unverified before building on it
Repeat it with extra confidence added on top
items.explanation: Honest labeling keeps it from silently carrying weight.

items.prompt: Under time pressure, what happens to the habit?

It shrinks and becomes explicit
It becomes stricter and slower
It passes to someone else
items.explanation: A quick partial check plus a clear flag still beats nothing.

items.prompt: Which statement is honest under time pressure?
choices: I believe X, but I have not confirmed it
X is settled, since the AI said so
X is certainly true, as far as I know it
X is verified, and the matter is now closed
items.explanation: It states what is believed and what is not checked.

items.prompt: Is time pressure a reason to hide that a check was skipped?
choices: Yes, to avoid worrying the whole group
Yes, if the claim turns out right
Yes, since nobody could verify it anyway
No, only a reason to shrink the check
items.explanation: Shrinking the check is fine; concealing the skip is not.

items.prompt: In Ines's step list, what comes right before acting?

Deleting the AI's whole answer
Comparing the claim to the source
Asking a second AI to confirm it
items.explanation: The order is read, isolate the claim, pick a source, compare, then act.

items.explanation: It needs documentation or an experiment, which takes more effort and know-how.

items.prompt: Timing a sort on lists of growing size shows the time growing faster than a straight line. How does that bear on the claim "it is O(n)"?
choices: It proves it right, since larger lists take longer to sort
It is evidence against it, and the docs would add confidence
It is irrelevant, since timing says nothing about growth rates
It proves a different exact formula for the sort routine
items.explanation: Super-linear growth contradicts a linear claim. One experiment is evidence, not proof, so documentation helps.
items.reference:
When checking is hard or short
📚 Hard claim: docs or a small experiment; one check may only narrow it
⏱️ Short on time: shrink the check, say what is unverified
🏷️ Cannot check: label it unverified before anything builds on it
Why: the habit bends with difficulty and time, but never to the point of presenting an unchecked claim as checked.
items.learnMore:
Bending the habit honestly

Hard claims need a different kind of check and sometimes more than one. Under time pressure the check shrinks and the flag becomes explicit.

Common mistake

Using time pressure to justify staying silent about what was not checked.
items.reflection: Think of a claim in your own field that is hard for an outsider to verify. What would an honest, shrunken version of the check look like?

items.prompt: In a live meeting you must mention an AI claim you cannot check in time. Which line fits the habit?
choices: This is unverified, so please confirm it before relying on it
This is a fact, because the assistant stated it very firmly
This is surely correct, and no one at all needs to check it
This is not worth mentioning at all in the meeting today
items.explanation: It states the claim and its status, so listeners know how much weight it can bear.

items.prompt: After one check on a hard claim, you are still not sure. What is a sensible next step?
choices: Stop, since one check always settles the whole matter
Re-ask the assistant until it finally agrees with you
Drop the claim, since hard claims cannot be checked
A second independent check, since one may only narrow it
items.explanation: For hard claims one check often narrows rather than settles, so a second independent one adds real value.

items.prompt: A colleague stated an unchecked AI claim as fact and it was right. Why is it still a process problem?
choices: Correct claims should always include a full citation list of sources
Nothing at all; a correct claim has no process problem to fix
Listeners could not tell it from the claims that were checked
They should have stayed silent until it was fully verified by all
items.explanation: Honesty about status lets others weigh the claim; a lucky hit teaches nothing about the next one.
